hello.title: Hello, C++
hello.summary: Write your first C++ program and print text and numbers with `std::cout`.
hello.lesson.0: Every C++ program starts in a function called `main`. Here is a complete program that prints one line of text.
hello.lesson.2: The first line, `#include <iostream>`, loads the part of the standard library that handles input and output. Without it, the compiler does not know `std::cout`.
hello.lesson.3: `int main()` is the start of the program. The curly braces `{` and `}` contain its statements. `std::cout` is the standard output, usually the terminal, and `<<` sends a value to it. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.
hello.lesson.5: You can chain `<<` to print several values in one statement. Text goes in double quotes, numbers do not. C++ calculates `2 + 3` before it prints the result. Text after `//` is a comment: the compiler ignores it.
hello.lesson.8: `std::cout` does not start a new line by itself. Inside a string, `\n` is the newline character. Without it, the next output continues on the same line.
hello.lesson.10: `std::endl` also ends the line, and in addition it **flushes** the output: it sends everything to the screen right away. This makes it slower, so most programs use `"\n"` and keep `std::endl` for the moments when the output must appear immediately.
hello.lesson.11: In `main`, you can leave out `return 0;`. The program then reports success automatically.
hello.lesson.12: C++ is case-sensitive: `Main` or `std::Cout` do not work. If you forget a `;`, the compiler stops with an error. Read the first error message carefully: it shows the line number.
hello.card.1: `int main() { ... }` is where the program starts
hello.card.3: `"\n"` ends the line, `std::endl` ends it and flushes
hello-1.explain: Output goes to `std::cout`, and the operator `<<` points in the direction the data flows: into the output.
hello-2.explain: The text is printed as it is. `4 + 5` has no quotes, so C++ calculates it and prints `9`.
hello-3.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. What do they print?
hello-3.explain: The first statement does not end the line, so `cd` continues right after `ab`.
hello-4.statement: `std::endl` ends the line and also flushes the output.
hello-4.explain: Both `"\n"` and `std::endl` end the line, but only `std::endl` also flushes, which is slower.
hello-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program can use `std::cout`.
hello-5.explain: `std::cout` is declared in the header `<iostream>`, the library for input and output.
hello-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the output is on two lines.
hello-6.explain: The newline character is written with a backslash: `\n`, inside quotes.
hello-7.prompt: Build a line that prints `Hi!` and ends the line with `std::endl`.
hello-7.explain: First comes `std::cout`, then each value with its own `<<`, and a `;` at the end.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Ready` and then `Go`.
hello-8.explain: The `#include` comes first, then `main`. Statements run from top to bottom, so `Ready` comes before `Go`.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
hello-9.pairs.2: sends a value to the output
hello-10.explain: The statement on line 3 has no `;` at the end. Write `std::cout << "Hello\n";`.
hello-11.explain: `"3 + 4"` is text in quotes, so it is printed as it is. The second `3 + 4` has no quotes, so it is calculated.
hello-12.statement: `Std::cout << "Hi";` also prints `Hi`, because C++ does not care about upper and lower case.
hello-12.explain: C++ is case-sensitive. The name is `std::cout`, all in lower case.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables of type `int`, `double`, `char`, `bool` and `std::string`, and use `auto` and `const`.
variables.lesson.0: A variable is a named place for a value. In C++ every variable has a **type**, which you write before the name. The type `int` holds whole numbers.
variables.lesson.2: You write the type only once, when you create the variable. After that, `=` gives the variable a new value. The type never changes: `age` is always an `int`.
variables.lesson.4: `double` holds numbers with a decimal point. `char` holds one character in single quotes. `bool` is either `true` or `false`. For text, use `std::string` with double quotes; it needs `#include <string>`.
variables.lesson.6: `std::cout` prints `true` as `1` and `false` as `0`. Send `std::boolalpha` to the output first if you want the words.
variables.lesson.9: With `auto`, the compiler works out the type from the value: `auto count = 3;` makes an `int`, and `auto half = 0.5;` makes a `double`. With `const`, a variable becomes read-only: changing it later is a compile error.
variables.lesson.11: You can also create a variable with braces: `int score{10};`. Braces protect you from losing data: `int n{2.5};` is an error, while `int n = 2.5;` cuts off the `.5` and stores `2`.
variables.lesson.12: Always give a variable a value when you create it. Inside a function, `int x;` has no defined value, and reading it is an error that the compiler may not catch. Also note: `auto text = "hi";` does not make a `std::string`, so write `std::string` when you want text.
variables.card.0: `int n = 5;` whole number, `double d = 2.5;` decimal number
variables.card.1: `char c = 'A';` one character, `bool b = true;` yes or no
variables.card.3: `auto x = 3;` lets the compiler pick the type
variables.card.4: `const int max = 10;` can not be changed
variables-1.prompt: Match each type to what it holds.
variables-1.pairs.1: a number with a decimal point
variables-2.explain: `a + 3` uses the old value `7`. The result `10` becomes the new value of `a`.
variables-4.prompt: Which line creates a variable that holds a single character?
variables-4.explain: A `char` gets a character in single quotes. Double quotes make text, and `x` without quotes is a name.
variables-5.statement: After `const double pi = 3.14;` you can write `pi = 3.0;` to change it.
variables-5.explain: `const` makes the variable read-only. Assigning a new value is a compile error.
variables-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the variable holds text.
variables-6.explain: Text in double quotes is stored in a `std::string`. A `char` holds only one character.
variables-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the compiler works out the type by itself.
variables-7.explain: In C++, `auto` lets the compiler deduce the type from the value. `var` and `let` come from other languages.
variables-8.prompt: Build a line that creates a `double` variable named `price` with the value `9.99`.
variables-8.explain: First the type, then the name, then `=` and the value. `int` can not hold `9.99`, and quotes would make text.
variables-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `16`.
variables-9.explain: A variable must exist before you use it: first `width`, then `area`, then print `area`.
variables-10.explain: Text needs double quotes. Single quotes are only for one `char`. Write `std::string name = "Bob";`.
variables-11.explain: `x` is an `int` and `y` is a `double`. When you multiply them, the result is a `double`: `5 * 2.5` is `12.5`.
variables-12.explain: With braces, C++ refuses to lose the `.5` and stops with an error. Only `int n = 2.5;` would store `2`.
decisions.title: Operators and decisions
decisions.summary: Calculate with arithmetic operators, compare values and choose what to do with `if`, `else` and `switch`.
decisions.lesson.0: C++ calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. The operator `%` gives the **remainder** of a division.
decisions.lesson.2: When both numbers are `int`, `/` is **integer division**: it cuts off the decimal part, so `7 / 2` is `3`. The remainder `7 % 2` is `1`. As soon as one number is a `double`, the result is a `double`: `7.0 / 2` is `3.5`. Never divide an `int` by `0`: the result is undefined.
decisions.lesson.4: Comparisons give a `bool`: `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. You combine conditions with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not).
decisions.lesson.6: Put comparisons in parentheses when you print them. Without them, C++ reads `<<` first and the code does not compile.
decisions.lesson.8: `if` runs a block only when its condition is `true`. The `else` block runs when it is `false`. With `else if` you check another condition. C++ checks from top to bottom and runs only the first block that matches.
decisions.lesson.10: `=` assigns a value, `==` compares. `if (x = 5)` sets `x` to `5` and is always true. The compiler warns you, so read the warnings.
decisions.lesson.12: `switch` compares one value with several `case` labels. `break` ends a case; without it, the program **falls through** and also runs the next case. `default` runs when no case matches.
decisions-1.explain: Both numbers are `int`, so `/` cuts off the decimal part: `17 / 5` is `3`.
decisions-2.explain: `5` fits into `17` three times (`15`), and `2` is left over. `%` gives this remainder.
decisions-3.explain: `x > 5` is already true, so the first block runs. The other branches are skipped, even though `x > 8` is also true.
decisions-4.explain: A single `=` assigns `5` to `x`. To compare, write `if (x == 5)`.
decisions-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `even`.
decisions-5.explain: A number is even when the remainder of the division by `2` is `0`, and `%` gives the remainder.
decisions-6.prompt: Fill the gap so `Done` is printed only when both `saved` and `closed` are `true`.
decisions-6.explain: `&&` is true only when both sides are true. `||` would also be true when only one side is true.
decisions-7.prompt: Build the first line of an `if` that checks whether `age` is at least `18`.
decisions-7.explain: The condition goes in parentheses after `if`, and the block starts with `{`. The operator is `>=`, not `=>`.
decisions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `Big`.
decisions-8.explain: First create `n`, then the `if` with its block, then the `else` block. `50 > 10` is true, so `Big` is printed.
decisions-9.prompt: Match the operator to its meaning.
decisions-9.pairs.3: at least one condition is true
decisions-10.prompt: This program should print `Perfect` only for a score of 100. Which line has the bug?
decisions-10.explain: `score = 100` assigns instead of comparing, so the condition is always true. Write `if (score == 100) {`.
decisions-11.explain: C++ calculates from left to right: `10 / 4` is `2` with integer division, and `2 * 2` is `4`.
decisions-12.explain: There is no `break` after `case 1`, so the program falls through and also runs the code of `case 2`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with `for` and `while` loops and visit every character of a string with a range-based `for`.
loops.lesson.0: A loop repeats code. A `for` loop has three parts in its parentheses, separated by `;`: a start, a condition and a step.
loops.lesson.2: `int i = 0` runs once at the start. Before every round, the loop checks `i < 3`. After every round, `i++` adds `1` to `i`. When the condition is `false`, the loop ends, so `i` takes the values `0`, `1` and `2`.
loops.lesson.3: Short forms: `i++` adds 1, `i--` subtracts 1, `x += 5` means `x = x + 5`. The same works with `-=`, `*=` and `/=`.
loops.lesson.6: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. Use it when you do not know in advance how many rounds you need.
loops.lesson.8: Make sure the condition becomes `false` at some point. If nothing in the loop changes `n`, the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.9: Two keywords control a loop from the inside: `break` leaves the loop at once, and `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one.
loops.lesson.12: A range-based `for` visits every item of a collection, from the first to the last. A `std::string` is a collection of characters, so `for (char c : word)` gives you one character after another. In the world about vectors, you use the same loop for lists of values.
loops.card.1: `while (n > 0) { ... }` repeats while the condition is true
loops.card.3: `break` leaves the loop, `continue` goes to the next round
loops-1.explain: `i` takes the values `0`, `1`, `2` and `3`: four rounds, so four stars on one line.
loops-2.explain: `i` is `2`, `4` and `6`, because the step is `i += 2`. Their sum is `12`.
loops-3.explain: `n` becomes `3`, `9`, `27` and `81`. Then `n < 50` is false and the loop stops.
loops-4.explain: The loop starts at `3` and counts down with `i--`. When `i` is `0`, `i > 0` is false, so `0` is not printed.
loops-5.explain: Starting at `0` with `i < 5` gives the values `0` to `4`: five rounds. With `<=` it would be six.
loops-6.statement: The loop `for (char c : word)` visits the characters of `word` from the first to the last.
loops-6.explain: A range-based `for` goes through the collection in order, from the first item to the last.
loops-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the loop prints every character of `name` on its own line.
loops-7.explain: A range-based `for` uses a colon: `for (char c : name)`.
loops-8.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints only `1`, `2` and `3`.
loops-8.explain: `break` leaves the loop. `continue` would only skip `4` and then print `5` to `10`.
loops-9.prompt: Build the first line of a loop that counts from 1 to 10.
loops-9.explain: Start at `1` and keep going while `i <= 10`, so `10` is included.
loops-10.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. Put them in order so the program prints `3`, `2`, `1` and then `Go!`.
loops-10.explain: Print `n` first, then make it smaller. After the loop ends, `Go!` is printed once.
loops-11.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
loops-11.pairs.4: goes on with the next round
loops-12.prompt: This program should print `0`, `1` and `2`. Which line has the bug?
loops-12.explain: With `i <= 3` the loop also runs for `3`. Write `while (i < 3) {`.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with parameters and return values, pass values by copy or by reference and overload functions.
functions.lesson.0: A function is a named block of code that you can call again and again. You write the return type, the name and the parameters in parentheses. The return type `void` means the function gives nothing back.
functions.lesson.2: Parameters are the values a function receives. `return` ends the function and sends a value back to the place where it was called. You can use that value like any other value.
functions.lesson.4: The compiler reads your file from top to bottom, so a function must be known before you call it. Either define it above `main`, or write a **declaration** above `main`: the first line of the function followed by `;`. The full definition can then come later.
functions.lesson.7: Normally a parameter gets a **copy** of the value. Changes inside the function do not change the variable of the caller. With `&` after the type, the parameter is a **reference**: another name for the caller's variable, so changes are visible outside.
functions.lesson.9: Copying a long `std::string` costs time. Use `const std::string& s` as the parameter: the function reads the original without copying it and can not change it.
functions.lesson.10: A function with a return type other than `void` must always reach a `return` with a value. If it can end without one, the result is undefined.
functions.lesson.12: Several functions can have the same name if their parameters differ. This is called **overloading**. The compiler picks the function whose parameter types fit the arguments.
functions.card.0: `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`
functions.card.2: `void f(int& n)` can change the caller's variable
functions-1.explain: The inner call `add(3, 4)` runs first and gives `7`. Then `add(2, 7)` gives `9`.
functions-2.explain: `x` is a reference to `score`, so `x = 0` changes `score` itself.
functions-3.explain: `x` is a copy of `n`. The function changes only the copy and returns `10`, so `n` stays `5`.
functions-4.explain: `2.5` is a `double`, so the compiler picks the overload with the `double` parameter.
functions-5.prompt: You want to call a function in `main`. Where must the function be declared?
functions-5.options.0: Above `main`, as a definition or a declaration
functions-5.options.1: Anywhere in the file, the order does not matter
functions-5.explain: The compiler reads from top to bottom. It must know the function before the call, either from the full definition or from a declaration.
functions-6.statement: A function with the return type `void` can give back a number with `return 5;`.
functions-6.explain: `void` means the function returns nothing. To return a number, use a return type like `int`.
functions-7.prompt: Fill the gap so `increase` changes the variable of the caller.
functions-7.explain: `int& n` makes `n` a reference to `count`, so `n++` changes `count`.
functions-8.prompt: Fill the gap so the function gives back the bigger number.
functions-8.explain: `return a;` ends the function and gives `a` back to the caller.
functions-9.prompt: Build the first line of a function `add` that takes two `int` values and returns an `int`.
functions-9.explain: The return type comes first, then the name, then the parameters in parentheses. `void` would mean: no return value.
functions-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `8`.
functions-10.explain: The function must be defined before `main` calls it. `cube(2)` is `2 * 2 * 2`, which is `8`.
functions-11.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
functions-11.pairs.2: a reference to the caller's variable
functions-12.explain: The function returns a number, so its return type must be `int`, not `void`. Write `int add(int a, int b) {`.
containers.title: Vectors and strings
containers.summary: Store many values in a `std::vector`, loop over them and work with the methods of `std::string`.
containers.lesson.0: A `std::vector` holds a list of values of one type. You write the type in angle brackets, for example `std::vector<int>`. A vector can grow while the program runs. It needs `#include <vector>`.
containers.lesson.2: `push_back` adds a value at the end, and `size()` gives the number of elements. With `v[i]` you get the element at index `i`. Indexes start at `0`, so the last index is `size() - 1`. `back()` gives the last element and `pop_back()` removes it.
containers.lesson.3: `v[i]` does not check the index. Reading outside the vector is undefined behaviour. `v.at(i)` checks the index and stops the program with an error when it is wrong.
containers.lesson.5: A range-based `for` visits every element. If you also need the index, count with a normal `for` loop. `size()` returns the type `std::size_t`, a whole number that can not be negative, so use it for the index too.
containers.lesson.7: In `for (int n : nums)`, `n` is a copy of each element. To change the elements themselves, use a reference: `int& n`.
containers.lesson.10: A `std::string` has useful methods too. `size()` gives the number of characters and `s[i]` one character. `+` joins two strings. `substr(start, count)` cuts out a part, and `find` gives the position where some text starts.
containers.lesson.12: `+=` adds text at the end, and `==` compares two strings. `std::to_string` turns a number into text, so you can join it with other text.
containers-1.explain: The vector starts with three elements, and `push_back` adds a fourth.
containers-2.explain: Indexes start at `0`: `v[0]` is `10`, so `v[1]` is `20`.
containers-3.explain: `substr(1, 3)` starts at index `1` (the `e`) and takes three characters.
containers-4.explain: The loop adds every element to `sum`: `2 + 4 + 6` is `12`.
containers-5.prompt: Which line adds `7` at the end of the vector `v`?
containers-5.explain: Vectors add elements at the end with `push_back`. The other forms do not exist for `std::vector`.
containers-6.statement: The first element of a vector `v` is `v[1]`.
containers-6.explain: Indexes start at `0`, so the first element is `v[0]`.
containers-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `3`.
containers-7.explain: `size()` gives the number of elements of a vector. A vector has no `length()` method.
containers-8.prompt: Fill the gap so the loop doubles every number in the vector.
containers-8.explain: Only a reference `int&` changes the elements themselves. With `int` or `auto`, `n` is a copy, and `const` forbids changes.
containers-9.prompt: Build a line that creates a vector `v` with the numbers `1`, `2` and `3`.
containers-9.explain: The element type goes in angle brackets, and the values go in curly braces.
containers-10.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. Put them in order so the program prints `Hi, Ann` and then `Hi, Ben`.
containers-10.explain: Create the vector first, then add `Ann` before `Ben`. The loop at the end prints the names in this order.
containers-11.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
containers-12.prompt: This program should print the last element. Which line has the bug?
containers-12.explain: The vector has three elements, so the last index is `2`. Write `v.at(2)` or `v.back()`.
classes.title: Classes and structs
classes.summary: Create your own types with `struct` and `class`: members, methods, constructors and `public` or `private` access.
classes.lesson.0: A `struct` groups several values into one new type. The values are called **members**. You reach a member with a dot: `p.x`.
classes.lesson.2: A `struct` or `class` definition ends with `};`. If you forget the `;` after the closing brace, the compiler shows an error, often on a later line.
classes.lesson.4: Functions inside a struct are called **methods**. They can use the members directly. A method marked `const` promises not to change the object.
classes.lesson.7: A `class` works like a `struct`, but its members are `private` by default: only the methods of the class can use them. After `public:`, everything can be used from outside. This protects the data from wrong changes.
classes.lesson.8: A **constructor** is a special method with the name of the class and no return type. It runs when you create an object and gives the members their first values, here with the list after the `:`. You can also give a member a default value directly, like `int count = 0;`.
classes.lesson.10: If you write `c.count = 100;` in `main`, the compiler stops with an error, because `count` is private. Only `increment` can change it, so the counter can only go up.
classes.lesson.11: Use `struct` for a simple group of data with public members. Use `class` when the object protects its data with private members and offers methods to work with it.
classes.lesson.12: Your own types work everywhere, also in a vector. In the loop, `const Item&` reads each element without copying it.
classes.card.0: `struct Point { int x; int y; };` groups data
classes.card.2: `class` members are `private` by default, `public:` opens them
classes.card.4: `int value() const { ... }` does not change the object
classes-1.explain: `b.w` is `2`, so `b.h` becomes `8`. The sum `2 + 8` is `10`.
classes-2.explain: `on` starts as `false`. Three toggles change it to `true`, `false` and `true` again.
classes-3.explain: The constructor sets `name` to `Kim` and `score` to `3`. After `addPoints(4)`, `score` is `7`.

classes-5.options.1: A method that deletes an object
classes-5.options.2: Any method that returns a value
classes-5.explain: A constructor has the name of the class and no return type. It gives a new object its first values.
classes-6.statement: In a `struct`, members are `public` by default.
classes-6.explain: That is the only difference between `struct` and `class`: in a `class`, members are `private` by default.

classes-11.pairs.3: only the class can use the members below

pointers.title: References and pointers
pointers.summary: Use references and pointers with `&` and `*`, check for `nullptr` and let `std::unique_ptr` manage memory for you.
pointers.lesson.0: A **reference** is a second name for an existing variable. After `int& ref = x;`, everything you do with `ref` happens to `x`.
pointers.lesson.2: A reference must get its variable when you create it, and it always stays connected to that variable. You already used references as parameters in the world about functions.
pointers.lesson.4: Every variable lives at an **address** in memory. A **pointer** is a variable that stores such an address. `&x` gives the address of `x`, `int*` is the type "pointer to `int`", and `*p` gives the value at the address in `p`.
pointers.lesson.6: `&` and `*` have two meanings. In a type, `int&` is a reference and `int*` is a pointer. In front of a variable, `&x` means "address of `x`" and `*p` means "the value `p` points to".
pointers.lesson.7: Unlike a reference, a pointer can later point to another variable. It can also point to nothing: that is the value `nullptr`. Always check for `nullptr` before you use `*p`.
pointers.lesson.9: Using `*p` when `p` is `nullptr`, or when it points to a variable that no longer exists, is undefined behaviour. The program may crash or print wrong values.
pointers.lesson.11: Sometimes you create an object whose lifetime you control yourself. In modern C++, `std::make_unique` from `<memory>` creates the object and gives you a `std::unique_ptr`. It owns the object and deletes it automatically at the end of its block. With `->` you reach a member through a pointer. The method `~Robot()` is a **destructor**: it runs when the object is deleted.
pointers.lesson.13: In old C++ code you see `new` and `delete`. If you forget `delete`, the memory is never given back. Prefer `std::make_unique`: the `std::unique_ptr` cleans up for you.
pointers.card.0: `int& r = x;` is another name for `x`
pointers.card.2: `*p` is the value `p` points to, `p->m` a member
pointers-1.explain: `b` is another name for `a`, so `b += 4` changes `a` to `7`.
pointers-2.explain: `p` points to `x`. `*p * 2` is `12`, and `*p = ...` stores it in `x`.
pointers-3.explain: `p` first points to `a`, then to `b`. So `*p = 9` changes `b`, and `a` stays `1`.
pointers-4.explain: The first call sets `n` to `0` through the pointer. The second call gets `nullptr`, and the check skips the change.
pointers-5.prompt: Which line creates a pointer `p` to the variable `x`?
pointers-5.explain: A pointer has a type with `*` and stores an address, which you get with `&x`.
pointers-6.statement: A `std::unique_ptr` deletes its object automatically at the end of its block.
pointers-6.explain: That is the job of `std::unique_ptr`: it owns the object and deletes it when it goes out of scope.
pointers-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints `5`.
pointers-7.explain: `*p` gives the value that `p` points to. `p` and `&x` are addresses, and `&p` is the address of the pointer itself.
pointers-8.prompt: Fill the gap so `p` points to nothing.
pointers-8.explain: In C++, a pointer that points to nothing has the value `nullptr`. The other words come from other languages.
pointers-9.prompt: Build a line that creates a smart pointer `p` to an `int` with the value `10`.
pointers-9.explain: `std::make_unique<int>(10)` creates the `int` and returns a `std::unique_ptr`. `auto` takes over its type.
pointers-10.prompt: These lines are inside `main`. Put them in order so the program prints `11`.
pointers-10.explain: `n` must exist before you take its address. The change through `p` must happen before printing.
pointers-11.prompt: Match the code to its meaning.
pointers-12.prompt: This program should print `3`. Which line has the bug?
pointers-12.explain: A pointer needs an address, not a value. Write `int* p = &x;`.
